📺 WHY I'M NOT BUYING THE DIP – A MUCH BIGGER SELLOFF COMING? + $AAPL OVERREACTION? + $PLTR MORE DOWNSIDE + $TSLA REMAINS STRONG + SELL $NVDA / SEMIS INTO STRENGTH

The market is showing serious signs of weakness ahead of the election, and I'm not convinced we've seen the worst of this correction.

While some stocks have already been crushed, the broader market is only about 4% off its highs. That's not enough for me to start putting my "blood in the streets" account to work.

*

$SPY just gave us a classic Red Dog Reversal sell signal.

It tried to break higher, failed to hold the move, and sold off throughout the afternoon yesterday.

The $750 area remains critical, with $749 acting as an important downside reference. If that breaks, there isn't much meaningful support until the 200-day moving average.

$QQQ is already leading the market lower.

Less than a month ago, the Nasdaq was making all-time highs. Now it's testing its 200-day EMA, and the initial bounce hasn't shown convincing follow-through.

Yesterday's close below $683.45 was another warning sign.

*

So when do I start buying aggressively?

My first "blood in the streets" tier typically activates when the market is 5–7% below its highs, with additional capital deployed another 4–5% lower. We're not there yet.

Individual stocks may look like bargains, but many remain below their 8-day and 21-day moving averages. Cheap can always get cheaper!

*

$AAPL is the selloff an overreaction?

Apple is approaching its 100-day moving average around $323, with $321 another important reference.

There could be a tactical buying opportunity, but don't blindly catch a falling knife.

Let it establish a 5, 15, or 30-minute low, recover, and then consider buying against that low with defined risk.

*

I'm staying away from $PLTR.

The stock broke its wedge pattern after a failed breakout, and the technical damage is significant.

$163 is an important reference, with the 200-day moving average also coming into focus.

Just because a stock has fallen dramatically doesn't mean it can't go lower.

*

$TSLA is only one of the few names still showing relative strength!

I bought when Tesla reclaimed $387 and continue managing it as a swing position.

My stop remains at $387, while more active traders can use yesterday's $397 low as a tighter reference.

If Tesla can hold these levels through the election, it could remain a relative outperformer.

*

Meanwhile, I'm not chasing the bounce in $NVDA / semis.

#Nvidia had another push-through failure yesterday and closed near its lows. With the 200-day moving average and $205 area in focus, I'd rather sell #NVDA into strength than buy the opening rally.

$SNDK remains technically broken below its 200-day, while $MU is beginning to show weakness after holding up better than its peers.

*

There are a LOT of broken stocks out there, and some former market leaders have already been cut in half.

Look at $NBIS or $ASTS that everyone loved just a while ago. These were great trades, but the technical picture has completely changed.

False breakouts, failures to reclaim lower highs, and breakdowns below the 8/21-day moving averages were clear warning signs.

Just because a stock was a winner doesn't mean you should keep holding it as a swing trade.

Different sequence, different trend. When the technicals break down, get out of the way, protect your capital, and wait for a better setup.

*

So, again, there are too many broken charts and failed rallies to justify getting aggressive.

Election uncertainty and geopolitical headlines could create additional volatility, but we can't control those events.

What we CAN control is our risk.

Not every dip is a buying opportunity, and sometimes the best trade is simply staying out of the way.

The divergence in AI output weirdly may be the highest it’s ever been, even though adoption is the broadest it’s ever been. 

A few years ago the best productivity gains you could get, even in the most capability-aligned field (like coding), was maybe 30-50% better productivity if you were very good at it. You’d spend a decent chunk of time cleaning up the mistakes of models, the context windows were too limited to do any long running work, and the interfaces required highly synchronous interactions. 

Now, the models can do far longer tasks at a time with limited human interaction. The harnesses support agentic work that can take on these larger tasks. The models are trained on vastly better datasets for a growing array of domains so you have to intervene far less. And we have systems that better support working with many agents at once. 

In just a two year timespan, the upper limits on productivity gains have gone from 30-50% to now likely 5-10X depending on the field. So we’ve gone from an environment where living at the frontier vs. not paying attention at all could be an order of magnitude difference in your output.

This distance is only getting wider from here given the rate of progress we’re likely to see with RSI. Crazy times.
